title.title: Seymour's second-neighbourhood conjecture
title.subtitle: Claim: every oriented graph has a vertex with at least as many vertices at distance two as at distance one

plain: One-way friendships: someone always has at least as many friends-of-friends as friends

object.heading: Arcs point left to right; no loops, no 2-cycles

beats.text: One-way friendships: $v$ follows 2 vertices, and reaches 3 more in two steps
Seymour, 1990: in every such graph some vertex has at least as many at distance two
Known for tournaments since 1996. The claim covers every oriented graph

steps: Take a smallest network where nobody has enough friends-of-friends
Trimming links gives every group a strict inequality
A counting argument breaks that inequality: impossible

achievement.label: Seymour's second-neighbourhood conjecture (1990)
achievement.context: Known for tournaments (Fisher, 1996); the best general ratio was about 0.7155
achievement.note: Fifteen pages, elementary: easy for an expert to check

verify.detail: Twelve lines of definitions and one theorem; distance two is exactly the conjecture's
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean statement; we did not build it

voice.text: Follows go one way. Does someone always have as many friends of friends as friends?
A smallest counterexample would obey an inequality that a counting argument breaks.
Claimed: true for every oriented graph.
